prize_parts.citation: for visionary, densely patterned prose, grounded in a poetic foundation, that builds memory, the body and dream into an expansive metaphysical architecture, from Blinding to Solenoid

statement.case_for: My writer is unchanged. My citation is now narrower: it rests on the prose project, with the poetry named only as its foundation. In round 1 I wrote prose and poetry side by side. The exchange showed that my coverage of the poetry and early fiction is the weakest part of my assessment. A citation should claim only what the committee can defend. On the common criteria, Cărtărescu still seems to me the most complete case on the shortlist. The voice is hard to mistake for another writer's. The formal ambition lies in large structures that organise memory, the body and dream, so the imaginative depth and the form seem to be one thing. The project appears to deepen across volumes rather than repeat. This rests on public knowledge and the longlist descriptions, which I have not independently verified. It is a judgment about the work and not about how many colleagues share it. The chair asked what would show that the length is earned. The test I would apply is whether recurring images and structural returns in Blinding and Solenoid bear weight or merely accumulate. From public knowledge I think they bear weight, but I cannot confirm that from here, and I hold it as a condition on my vote and not a settled fact.
statement.case_against: The reservations from round 1 stand, and the exchange has not removed them. First, I judge dense, rhythmic Romanian prose through translation, and I cannot assess what is lost. Second, the very long late books may be unevenly sustained, and the supplied evidence cannot settle that. Third, the whole-oeuvre judgment rests mainly on the late novels, so the narrower prose citation is the honest scope. Adonis presents the clearest and most documented remaking of a literary language. If the committee obtained credible Arabic-language readings showing that the later poetry holds the level of the major collections, my first-place ordering would face a real challenge. Carson's case is the easiest for the committee to examine directly in English. The risk to my own ranking is that I may be giving too much weight to imaginative scale. Scale can be overweighted when the most distinctive effects are the ones translation distorts.

responses.point: Olsson keeps Adonis first for a decades-long remaking of Arabic poetic language and keeps the citation on the poetry. He asks that the essays and public role not stand in for the literary case. He ranks Cărtărescu fourth because he doubts that the late volumes are evenly sustained.
responses.response: I agree that the citation for Adonis should stay with the poetry and say what is claimed, which is the renewal of poetic language and form. I also agree that translation exposure should not count more heavily against one candidate than another. I accept that part of my earlier argument was a judgment: I suggested that prose built on large-scale structure travels better than prosodic verse. I would not use it as a decisive reason. Where I still differ is on what the committee can currently verify. Your own uncertainty about the later poetry is an open question, and I cannot answer it. I support seeking Arabic-language and Romanian-language readings for both candidates under identical questions. If the readings favoured Adonis on sustained quality, I would reconsider. Without them I keep Cărtărescu first and Adonis as my first alternative.

responses.point: Sward keeps Carson first. She argues that continuity of concerns across forms (grief, desire, the fragment, the afterlife of ancient texts) answers the signal-books objection. She also argues that her English text is directly legible to the committee, and she would keep the citation on Carson's own writing.
responses.response: Your continuity argument answers part of my worry. I accept that recurring concerns across the essays, the verse novel and the elegy amount to development and not repetition. Directly testable English is a real advantage, and I weigh it. It lets the committee test the claim on the text, which cannot be done for the other leading candidates. My remaining hesitation is narrower than before. It concerns how much of the achievement a text-only citation can name when the book-object and layout elements carry part of the invention. I would not exclude Carson on that basis, and I keep her as my second alternative. I still place Cărtărescu first, on the view that his achievement lives wholly in the text and a single citation can name it. I recognise this is a weighting choice and not a demonstrated superiority.

responses.point: Mattson asks whether the late novels earn their length through structure or let scale substitute for it. She wants any citation to say plainly that the claim concerns the prose project and not the full poetic corpus. She also questions whether Carson's work is sustained depth or formal experiment.
responses.response: I take your scope point and have changed my citation to follow it. It now names prose and mentions poetry only as foundation. On the structure question, I offered a test: do the recurring images and structural returns carry weight or merely accumulate? I cannot verify the answer, and I would prefer that we state it as a condition and not assert it. We also share the Carson reservation. Sward's continuity argument reduces it for me but does not remove it. I would add that your uncertainty about poetry and early work matches mine, so we should not make claims about the whole poetic corpus.

responses.point: Palm separates two questions: uneven quality in some volumes, which can be tested against the major works, and translation loss, which determines whether the achievement is visible at all. She argues that the case rests on the Blinding trilogy and Solenoid and so survives some unevenness elsewhere. She asks that the committee say openly that the judgment is made through translation.
responses.response: I accept the distinction and find it useful. It lets me say that unevenness in minor volumes would not defeat a citation anchored to the major prose works. It also means a tighter citation is safer than a broad one. I would not stretch your argument too far, though. The question of evenness within the long late books is not only about minor volumes, because Solenoid itself is among the longest works. The condition applies to the books carrying the case. I agree that a recommendation should state openly that it rests on translation and on public knowledge that none of us has independently verified.

responses.point: Sem-Sandberg says he would move toward Carson or Adonis if evidence beyond the best-known Cărtărescu volumes proved thin. He agrees that the prose should carry the citation and the poetry should be secondary. He keeps Magris at fifth for lack of formal intensity.
responses.response: I share the conditionality and treat it as a real part of my position and not a formality. Our agreement on citation scope is helpful, but it is not evidence of merit. I would add one point to the Magris discussion. His case rests on erudition, historical imagination and a coherent Central European subject, which are real strengths, and I do not think the formal intensity matches the leading three. My own background in non-fiction is context only and does not move my judgment. I would not move him ahead of the leading three.

uncertainties: How much of the density, rhythm and wordplay of Cărtărescu's Romanian prose survives translation is unknown, and I cannot verify translation quality.
Whether the very long late novels, including Solenoid, are evenly sustained cannot be settled from the supplied evidence. This is a condition on my position.
My coverage of the poetry and early fiction is partial, so the recommendation is scoped to the prose project and the whole-oeuvre judgment rests mainly on the late novels.
Whether Arabic-language readings would show that Adonis's later poetry holds the level of his major collections is unresolved and could change my ordering.
How a text-only citation should treat Carson's book-object and layout elements, and how to separate her scholarship and translation from her original writing, remains open.
I have not independently verified any source. I rely on public knowledge and the supplied longlist descriptions.
Whether a co-opted member votes in the committee is undocumented. My simulated vote is a modeling assumption, and this recommendation is not a decision of the full Academy.
statement.conflict_note: No conflict requiring recusal is apparent from the supplied profile. It records no personal, professional or archival tie to any shortlisted writer. It records only biographical and collegial connections that do not involve the candidates. I was elected alongside Steve Sem-Sandberg in 2020. I am married to former finance minister Pär Nuder. My Nobel biography drew on Nobel Foundation and family archives. I have been Permanent Secretary since 1 June 2026. My background in non-fiction and biography is context and not evidence of preference for any candidate. The profile shows no change since round 1.
